item.description:
Authors: Hongyu Li, Zhan Yu, Zhe Zhao, Kimmo Yan, Xiong Kuang, et al.

We propose Less is Safer (LIS), a compact yet highly effective dataset for safety alignment, constructed through interpretable feature-guided selection and adversarial synthesis. item.title: Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
item.description:
Authors: Xiaoyu Liang, Virginia Ceccatelli, Aliai Eusebi, Tobias Braun, Nils Loose, et al.

Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. item.title: A Mechanistic Interpretability Study of an Astronomy Foundation Model
item.description:
Authors: Rachel C. Zhang, Alberto Bietti, Wes Gurnee, Alessandro Favero, Miles Cranmer

Foundation models are increasingly used across the sciences, but whether their internal computations correspond to known scientific operations or proceed through different mechanisms remains unclear. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for assessing reliability, identifying failure modes, and learning new science from the models. We present, to our knowledge, the first causal mechanistic interpretability study of an astronomy foundation model, AION-1, focusing on its multimodal advantage

item.description:
Authors: Zhimin Hu, Chen Jiang, Hanbo Xie, N. Apurva Ratan Murty, Sashank Varma

Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. item.description:
Authors: Lorenzo Cirillo, Irene Amerini, Andrea Cavallaro

Deep neural networks underpin fundamental tasks in a wide range of signal domains, such as image, audio, and language processing. However, their internal mechanisms are notably difficult to interpret. Internal activations are structured signals transformed across layers that may encode a multitude of interdependent relationships, as individual neurons frequently represent multiple underlying concepts. Understanding the internal representations of neural networks and characterizing their relationship with human conceptual structure are two critical questions for elucidating model mechanisms. The former reveals how learned knowledge is organized in internal representations, whereas the latter provides a basis for interpreting these representations through human conceptual structure. item.title: A Geometric Invariant of Attention Predicts Head Specialization from Weights Alone
item.description:
Authors: Miguel P. Bento

Transformers are built with continuous symmetries in the attention mechanism. We derive $ρ$, a scalar invariant that measures each head's capacity to couple to rotary positional encodings. item.description:
Authors: Yuji Nozawa, Yu-Chieh Lin, Youyang Ng

Self-supervised learning in Vision Transformer models, such as DINO, enables robust visual perception without requiring labeled data by leveraging large-scale image datasets. However, these models lack a focusing mechanism during training, resulting in perceptual representations that are often ambiguous or overly similar. item.description:
Authors: Nika Zahedi, Fangyi Zhu, Anna Wu

Lenses that decode hidden states into words are a popular way to look inside language models, but a heatmap of decoded words only shows what a vector reads as and cannot distinguish whether, or how much, the model uses the information. We present an interactive viewer that puts reading, tracing and editing on the same layers-by-tokens grid of the residual stream. item.description:
Authors: Vitus Benson, Fanny Yang, Markus Reichstein

Earth observation foundation models produce global metre-resolution embeddings that underpin work across agriculture, ecology, hydrology, and beyond. Yet these embeddings are opaque: each dimension entangles unrelated physical concepts, which makes them difficult to interpret and their robustness hard to assess. item.description:
Authors: Linkai Peng, Baorian Nuchged, Yuyang Yao

Audio language model benchmarks provide comprehensive evaluation across diverse tasks. However, some tasks can be answered from the transcript or even the question alone, and benchmark scores can therefore confound acoustic understanding with language modeling ability. item.title: Probing Transformer Representations Layer by Layer, Module by Module
item.description:
Authors: Ambroise Odonnat, Theo Gnassounou, Laetitia Chapel, Romain Tavenard, Ievgen Redko

Which representation should be probed in a transformer-based foundation model? Recent work shows that the standard practice of probing the final layer is often suboptimal, as intermediate layers can provide better features. Yet, representations are still largely studied along depth alone, treating each transformer block as an atomic unit. item.title: Dropping Tokens Without Dropping Them: Causal Attribution for Diabetic Retinopathy
item.description:
Authors: Pramath Girish Haritz, Chandra Sekhar Seelamantula

In this work, we investigate whether attention-based attribution maps in a vision transformer provide causal explanations for diabetic retinopathy (DR) classification. We introduce a principled decomposition of attention into two attribution maps: the contribution ($c_t$), which satisfies the completeness axiom in explainable artificial intelligence (xAI), and the pull ($p_t$), which quantifies causal explanations. item.title: SWEET: Mitigating Spurious Feature Reliance in LLM Reasoning via Weight Editing
item.description:
Authors: Zhizhang Fu, Lucas Zhao, Michalis Korakakis, Mengru Ding, Lukasz Szpruch, et al.

Reasoning in large language models can be disrupted by simple input perturbations (e.g. adding irrelevant distractors), suggesting reliance on spurious correlations. Identifying and suppressing the spurious features involved in long chain-of-thought reasoning remains challenging. We introduce Spurious-feature WEight EdiTing (SWEET), a training-free method that combines counterfactual interventions with mechanistic interpretability to identify and suppress spurious-features. Tags: features, reasoning

item.title: Can small transformers learn the language of Coxeter groups?
item.description:
Authors: J. Elisenda Grigsby, Yiyao Huang, Arushi Katyal, Ryan Lin, Pranav Ramakrishnan, et al.

The field of mechanistic interpretability is well-suited to collaborative projects between mathematicians and AI researchers. This work describes one such project. We trained a small transformer to learn the language of the Coxeter group affine A2, best known as the symmetries of the tiling of the Euclidean plane by equilateral triangles. We then formulated and proved a word-theoretic conjecture about affine A2 after observing the attention patterns of the trained model.

Tags: attention

item.description:
Authors: Yair Cohen, Scott M. Gilmore

Deep neural networks achieve universal function approximation by stacking interconnected nonlinearities, but as a consequence they are sensitive to noise and resist mechanistic interpretation. In contrast, the local update rules of cellular automata, such as Conway's Game of Life, give rise to not merely interpretable but programmable dynamics. item.title: Represented but Not Used: Value-Policy Dissociation in LLM Agents
item.description:
Authors: Yuzhang Luo, Mohamed Aghzal, Liangming Pan, Ziyu Yao

Large language model (LLM) agents need to choose actions whose consequences unfold over multiple future steps, yet poor decisions do not reveal whether the model failed to represent those consequences or failed to use them. Mechanistic interpretability has studied internal representations of environment state and plans, but sequential decision making also requires evaluating how candidate actions change future outcomes. item.title: Detecting and Explaining Robot Policy Failures from Sparse Internal Features
item.description:
Authors: Riad Ahmed, Sujosh Nag, Moniruzzaman Akash, Momotaz Begum

Visuomotor policies can handle many robot manipulation tasks, but understanding their failures remains difficult. Unfamiliar conditions and small action errors can lead to failure, yet watching the robot alone tells us little about what went wrong inside the policy. We introduce MIND (Mechanistic Interpretability for Neural Diagnosis), a method that looks inside a trained policy to detect failures during execution and identify the internal concepts involved. Authors: Jinchi Zhu, Tie Luo

Foundation models pretrained on similar data distributions tend to learn overlapping semantic structure, but their representations are distinct due to different model architecture, pretraining objectives and protocols. item.title: The Truth Beneath the Tokens: Prompt-Space Recovery of Knowledge Edits in Language Models
item.description:
Authors: Manit Baser, Rachel Yeo Hui Min, Aditya Nawal, Dinil Mon Divakaran, Mohan Gurusamy

Model editing provides an efficient way to update factual knowledge in transformer models. Recent approaches reverse edits by modifying, masking, or decomposing model weights, but make recovery dependent on weight-space interventions. We instead show that pre-edit knowledge can be recovered through input-space interventions alone, without modifying the edited model's weights. item.title: Cross-Layer TopK: Dynamically Allocating Sparsity Across Layers in Transcoders
item.description:
Authors: Anyuan Zhuo, Shaohua Zhang, Tianle Li, Yuan Lin, Diandian Gu, et al.

Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) decompose the activations of large language models into human-interpretable features and trace how these features interact across layers to form circuits, making them a key tool for mechanistic interpretability. However, training CLTs effectively and efficiently is hard. item.title: Calibrated concept profiles: making the reading of a model's neurons a measurement
item.description:
Authors: Piotr Wilam

Interpretability has largely moved from reading a model's neurons directly to reading a second model trained on the first: a probe, a sparse autoencoder, a crosscoder. The move answered real faults -- mixed meanings, thresholds without a unit, readings that did not transfer from one study to the next -- but gave up what a direct reading alone provides: nothing trained in between, the neurons themselves named, and a reading that can be repeated and compared. item.title: Localizing and Editing the Goal Representation of a Vision-Language-Action Model
item.description:
Authors: Sudhanshu Srivastava, Faisal Aqlan

Operators can state safety constraints for robots as prohibitions such as "do not put the bowl on the stove". We study whether OpenVLA follows such prohibitions and where it represents the goal it executes. The 10 tasks of LIBEROGoal share one scene, so we can label the goal that each rollout executes. We combine closed-loop rollouts with activation patching, linear probes, activation steering and runtime monitors. On LIBERO-Goal, negation had no detectable effect on which task OpenVLA executed.

Tags: safety, probing, steering, vision

item.description:
Authors: Giuseppe Marra, Pierre Genevès, Meghyn Bienvenu, Thomas Schiex, Sylvie Thiébaux, et al.

We examine opportunities for neurosymbolic AI alongside increasingly powerful neural models, particularly with regards to efficiency, safety and interpretability. We identify two major challenges: ensuring semantic alignment between neural and symbolic components, and managing the computational cost of symbolic inference and learning. item.title: Uncertainty, Not Concealment: A Mechanistic Reappraisal of Sycophancy in Vision-Language Models
item.description:
Authors: Mohamed I. Eldagla, Zeyad H. ElShafei, Ahmed M. Anter

Vision-language models (VLMs) in medical retrieval-augmented generation must be able to say when a retrieved report contradicts the X-ray, so understanding whether they can detect such conflicts is important for safe deployment. The sycophancy mask hypothesis holds that these models internally detect conflicts but refuse to report them, concealing a detected contradiction. item.title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety
item.description:
Authors: Fazl Barez, Tung-Yu Wu, Hunar Batra, Gabriele Dominici, Florent Draye, et al.

Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. item.description:
Authors: Jacob Solinsky, Serguei Pakhomov

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an increasingly popular means of translating Large Language Model (LLM) hidden state vectors into a human-comprehensible list of features or symbols. item.title: User Embeddings are Superpositions of Interpretable Behavioral Modes
item.description:
Authors: Jonathan Kozaczuk, Zheng Dong, Noyan Evirgen, Keivan Majidi, Eddie K. H. Ng, et al.

User embeddings are central components of modern recommendation, personalization, and behavioral modeling systems. Though these embeddings can compactly encode rich behavioral information, they are inherently dense and opaque, limiting interpretability. To address this gap, we argue that user embeddings can be understood as sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes. item.title: Scaling Laws for SAE Training Data
item.description:
Authors: Nikita Koriagin, Nikita Balagansky, Daniil Gavrilov

Activation storage is often a bottleneck in sparse autoencoder (SAE) training. We study how many unique activations an SAE needs when its total training budget is fixed. Quality improves rapidly as the buffer grows, then reaches a plateau where replaying the buffer is nearly as effective as using fresh activations throughout training. Beyond this point, additional unique activations bring little benefit to reconstruction or interpretability, so the buffer need not grow with the training budget.

Tags: SAE

item.description:
